name: Emeka Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Anything you say stays confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman at Haldane Farm, 420 hectares, about 250 beef cattle and the rest in wheat and grass. Old Mr Haldane owns it, he's 68, and I've worked for him since I was 19, part-time through my degree and full-time after. I'm up at half five, feed and check the cattle, then whatever the day throws at me, fencing, the silage clamp, the vet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know exactly where I stand. Mr Haldane trusts me, the cattle are the best in the district, and I go home tired in a good way. What wears me out is the uncertainty about what happens when he retires, because none of his kids want the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So, more or less the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I didn't expect much and I wasn't wrong. I don't use any of it anyway, never have. At the pub I'd say the farm's the same as it was, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not AI that worries me, it's Mr Haldane selling up. If a big outfit buys it, they'll bring their own manager and maybe their own stockman. I'd find work, there's plenty round here, but I'd lose the best job I've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep saving. Ruth and I live in the farm cottage, and I own a small house in town that I rent out, so I'd keep that ticking over. And I'd finally ask Mr Haldane straight out what his plans are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about the farm changing hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked Mr Haldane already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't like asking things I might not want the answer to. He's not a big talker either. We've worked side by side for eight years and never once talked about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruth think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth thinks I should've asked two years ago. She works the counter at the farm merchant's in town, so she hears every bit of gossip about who's selling. Ruth says Haldane Farm comes up every time someone with a big tractor walks into the merchant's.

say: I'd say I **expected little** from AI and was right.
I'd tell people at the pub the **farm's the same**.
think: Privately I fear **Mr Haldane selling** the farm more than any AI.
A new owner could bring **their own stockman**, ending my best job.
do: Keep working and **saving** at the usual rate.
Keep the **rental house** in town let and maintained.
Finally ask Mr Haldane about his **retirement plans**.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about the farm **changing hands**.
S0.quote: Ruth says Haldane Farm comes up every time someone with a big tractor walks into the merchant's.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **succession** at the farm, unrelated to AI.
He avoids hard **conversations**, even after eight years.
A rental house and savings give him a solid **fallback**.
He has never used **AI tools** and feels no pull to start.

steps.text: Ask Mr Haldane directly about selling or handing on the farm
Keep saving monthly and keep the town house rented out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. Buying, booking, answering customers. That's Ruth's job, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch cattle much, which is true. I'd probably say the computers can have the paperwork, I never liked it. I wouldn't say much online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Ruth I'd think about. The merchant's counter is all orders, stock checks and answering farmers' questions, and that's exactly what they're saying the software takes. My job's fine for now, robots for cattle are a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep going at Haldane's. I'd talk Ruth into saving her whole wage for a while, and we'd live on mine, which we can. And I'd wait and see what the merchant's does before panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for Ruth. Not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new tools, if Mr Haldane asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He won't ask, he's worse than me. If a new owner made me, I'd do the minimum, record the weights and that's it. I'm good at cattle, not screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine for money, which is true. I'd also tell her to look at the vet practice, they always need people on the desk who know farmers. I'm not sure that desk survives either, mind.

say: I'd say this **barely touches cattle**, which is true.
I'd say computers can have the **paperwork** I never liked.
think: Privately I worry about **Ruth's counter job** at the merchant's.
Cattle **robots** feel a long way off for my own work.
do: Keep working at Haldane's and **keep my head down**.
Have Ruth **save her whole wage** while we live on mine.
**Wait and see** what the merchant's does before acting.
feel: He feels **anxious** for Ruth, but **not for himself**.
S1.quote: I'm good at cattle, not screens.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with his partner's **ordering and counter** work.
He'd do the **minimum** with any tool a new owner forced on him.
Strong savings let them live on **one wage** comfortably.
He suggests a job for Ruth while **doubting** it lasts.

steps.text: Carry on feeding and checking Haldane's cattle as usual
Bank Ruth's whole wage and live on his own pay
Hold off on big decisions until the merchant's changes are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots by 2031. That's the farm gone, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I don't believe it, at first. Then I'd say what everyone would say, that the government had better have a plan. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want someone to be in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ruth's job goes in 2028 and Mr Haldane sells to some robot outfit by 2030 or 2031. I'd be 31 with nothing I know how to do except cattle, and the cattle would be done by machines. The rental house and the savings would keep us going a few years, but I'd have no idea what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, the new truck I've been looking at, the holiday. I'd save every penny. And then, honestly, I'd keep working and wait, because I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Lying awake, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. Is there anything that would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Haldane told me he was selling, I'd go looking that week. There'd be other farms for a year or two. I just don't know if moving farms helps when they're all getting the same robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst moment you can picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Standing at the gate watching a machine feed my cattle would be the worst moment I can picture. The new owner would be telling me it does it cheaper than me. I've been at Haldane's since I was 19, and that would be the end of the only job I've ever wanted.

say: I'd say at first I **don't believe** it.
I'd say the **government** had better have a plan, though I don't march.
think: Privately I expect **Ruth's job** gone in 2028 and the farm sold by **2031**.
At 31, I'd only know **cattle**, and machines would do that.
do: **Save every penny** we can from both wages.
Keep working and **wait**, moving only if Mr Haldane sells.
S2.quote: Standing at the gate watching a machine feed my cattle would be the worst moment I can picture.
fieldNote: Both household incomes fall in sequence: **Ruth first**, then him.
He has savings and a house but **no plan** for what comes after.
His resistance shows as **waiting**, not as protest.
He sees no gain in **switching farms** if all automate.

steps.text: Cancel the new truck purchase and this year's holiday
Save both wages in full where possible
Stay at Haldane's until Mr Haldane says he's selling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. And the robots by 2034. Bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so use it properly. I'd say it to the lads I play football with, because half of them work on farms. I'd still not be posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 34 when the robots come for cattle work. That's enough time for Mr Haldane to retire and sell, and enough time for me to find something they won't automate first. I don't know what that is yet, which bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at the livestock inspector jobs with the council. Somebody has to check animal welfare on all these robot farms, and they'd want people who know cattle. I'd keep saving and I'd tell Ruth to start looking for something before her job goes, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would becoming an inspector mean learning computer systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and I'd hate that part. I'd do it if it kept me with cattle. That's the trade I'd have to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a contradiction, given you've never used any of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I know. I'd rather learn one computer screen than lose the cattle altogether. A screen I can live with, a life without cattle I'm not sure I can.

say: I'd tell my **football mates** on farms to use the time properly.
think: Privately at 34 robots arrive, and the **farm may sell** before that.
I don't yet know what job **won't be automated**, which bothers me.
do: Apply for **livestock inspector** jobs with the council.
Urge Ruth to find **new work** before hers goes.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but **less** than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I'd rather learn one computer screen than lose the cattle altogether.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him find a **cattle-linked** role that needs human judgement.
He accepts learning **one system** as the price of staying with animals.
He names his own **contradiction** openly.
Still no wider plan; his thinking stays **close to home**.

steps.text: Apply for council livestock inspector jobs within the year
Keep saving each month from both wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different thing. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so no point panicking. People would have plenty to say, and I'd mostly listen. That's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough for Mr Haldane to sell and for me to have a go at buying some of it. Land's dear, but with the house in town and the savings, maybe 50 hectares and part of the herd. Robots or no robots, it's better to own the land than work it for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Haldane whether he'd sell me the bottom fields and some cows when he retires, and give him a number. I'd keep working as normal till then. The rest I'd leave until it's closer, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use robots on your own 50 hectares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first. Maybe once everyone else has them and they're cheap and they work. I'm not going to be the first, I never am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you more confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work on someone else's farm for a couple of years. Ruth says I'm the last man in the district to get a smartphone, and she's right.

say: I'd say there's **time** to sort things, so no point **panicking**.
I'd mostly **listen** while others at the pub talked it through.
think: Privately ten years gives a chance to **buy part** of Haldane Farm.
**Owning land** beats working it for someone, robots or not.
do: Offer Mr Haldane a price for the **bottom fields** and some cows.
Keep working at Haldane's **as normal** until then.
Leave **robot decisions** until others have proved them.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, but it's a **long way off**.
S4.quote: Robots or no robots, it's better to own the land than work it for someone.
fieldNote: A long horizon finally prompts the **succession talk** he's avoided.
His assets make a **50-hectare** purchase plausible.
He'd adopt robots **last**, after seeing them proven.
The decade shifts his worry from job loss to **ownership**.

steps.text: Offer Mr Haldane a price for the bottom fields and cows
Keep running Haldane's cattle as normal meanwhile
Wait until neighbours prove robots work before buying any

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Ruth's job first, then mine, and the farm sold before I've worked out anything else. What would help is time, really, and some help for young farmers to buy land, because then at least we'd own something when the robots came.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the older farmers like Mr Haldane. They're the ones deciding what happens to the land. Whoever buys the old farms decides who gets to work on them.

headlineQuote: Whoever buys the old farms decides who gets to work on them.
portrait: Emeka is 27, **head stockman** at an old family beef farm, living with Ruth, who works a **merchant's counter**.
He has never used **AI tools** and prefers cattle to screens.
His biggest fear before AI is the owner **selling the farm** with no successor.
He reacts to change by **saving and waiting**, and avoids hard conversations.
With more time he plans to **buy land** and maybe become a livestock **inspector**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Ruth's job gone first, then his, and the farm **sold**.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, and help for young farmers to **buy land**.
